rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Lengthen only the gradient to test whether the crowded central pairs respond to slope. The current last peak at 7.16 minutes leaves room to improve resolution without likely exceeding the 10-minute scoring threshold.

The shallower gradient substantially improved the critical pair, but further lengthening risks a time penalty. Raise temperature by one step to test selectivity at that pair while bringing the last peak earlier.

Return to 40 C and use a shallower gradient to improve the slope-responsive critical pair. Raising the starting organic fraction trims the weak-solvent portion, aiming to keep the last peak within 10 minutes despite the longer gradient.
Injection 4 achieved the maximum CRF. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to test whether full resolution can be retained with an earlier last peak, keeping injection 4 as the benchmark.

Test whether a larger temperature increase moves the critical pair through its apparent selectivity crossover and restores separation in the reversed order. This may recover full resolution with a shorter retention window than injection 4.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness to improve the newly limiting pair at 55 C, while testing whether the neighboring central pair retains its resolution margin. The last peak should remain comfortably below 10 minutes.

Narrow the gradient further to bring the limiting pair above R = 1.5; the other central pair remained nearly unchanged in the previous slope test. Extrapolation places the last peak near 9 minutes, potentially matching the maximum score with faster elution than injection 4.

Test a lower starting organic fraction against injection 7 to shift selectivity in the limiting early-middle pair. If this restores full resolution despite the slightly steeper gradient, it may provide a faster alternative to injection 8.

Shorten injection 9 by one gradient-time step to seek a faster fully resolved separation. The early-middle pair has some resolution margin, while the temperature-reversed central pair has previously tolerated steeper gradients.

With the maximum CRF secured, explore a substantially faster high-temperature gradient. The limiting early-middle pair may cross and separate in reversed order as temperature and steepness increase; this run tests that alternative selectivity region.

Explore the low-temperature selectivity region, where central pairs may separate after a different elution-order crossover. The broad, moderately fast gradient should keep the last peak below 10 minutes while testing an alternative to the 55 C optimum.

Return to the fully resolved 40 C region and preserve injection 4's gradient slope while raising the starting organic fraction to shorten retention. This tests how much initial weak-solvent time can be removed before early peaks or the critical central pair lose resolution.

Test whether lowering the starting organic fraction can offset the early-middle resolution loss from a shorter gradient, as suggested by injections 7 and 9. This targets full resolution with the last peak earlier than injection 11's 8.00 minutes.

Reduce the endpoint by one step to lift injection 15's limiting pair above R = 1.5. The other central pair has little margin, so this tests whether both can remain resolved with a last-peak time below 8 minutes.

Raise temperature one step from the fastest fully resolved method to test whether it can shorten retention while maintaining resolution. This isolates temperature selectivity from the steep-gradient effects seen in injection 12.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to test whether the reversed critical pair separates further at 60 C while shortening retention. Monitor the first pair closely, since stronger initial solvent may compromise its resolution.
